#DeepfakeRegulation #Deepfakes #ITRules2026 #AIRegulation #IndiaAI https://t.co/WyvvRJRW7E

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Report: White House Fears UK Apple iCloud Backdoor Targets Trump, Farage | Ken Macon, Reclaim The Net

The New Statesman is reporting that a White House security official expects the UK to use the backdoor it wants to build into Apple's iCloud – through a secret court order – to spy on the Trump administration and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

The magazine said it had seen a message sent in September from the official to a colleague, which reads: "The UK is making another attempt to put a backdoor on iCloud. This time by their secret court. They're going to lean on a court order to justify it. They will use this back door to spy on the administration and Nigel Farage."

The report does not show that anyone has actually been spied on in this way, and it's obviously alarmist, but the message reveals the fear is present inside the US administration, so at least people are aware of what the UK is doing to undermine privacy.

It is also a perfect example of how a backdoor built to catch criminals is actually a tool that can be used by whoever happens to have it at their disposal, including against political opponents – and allies.

The UK is keeping the order so secret that Apple was able to brief the US Vice President about it - but not the US Congress.

The UK first tried to get Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, through the country's Investigatory Powers Act, and a secret technical capability notice (TCN). The order was later changed to cover only UK users, after the US put pressure on its ally.

Apple never built that backdoor, at least as far as we know. Instead, it withdrew its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users, and new UK users are still unable to turn it on.

Apple has also said that it has "never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will."

In June, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan wrote to UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to warn that if reports about the UK order were true, it would mean that the country is building "backdoors into their encrypted services."

Jordan said that would put at risk the security of US citizens' data.

In September, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Republican Representative Warren Davidson wrote to the UK’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal to express their concern over the secret order, saying that the UK was being “wholly inappropriate” in preventing Apple from discussing the issue with US Congress.

"The U.K. government's unprecedented demands for secrecy in this matter undermine democratic governance in both the United States and the U.K., and needlessly strain the relationship between our two nations," the two congressmen wrote.

Weakening encryption in consumer software, the letter said, “introduces critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited by hostile foreign actors.”

Apple went to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), which hears complaints about surveillance, to try to have the UK order revoked. Privacy International and Liberty have a separate challenge before the same court.

The UK government will neither confirm nor deny that the order exists. But Ben Jaffey KC, who represents Privacy International and Liberty, told the tribunal that "the horse has long bolted."

"The fact that Apple even needed to ask permission confirms there is a TCN," Jaffey said.

Meanwhile, Neil Sheldon KC, acting for the government, said the home secretary's position was "neither irrational nor unsupported by evidence."

In February 2025, Reclaim The Net reported that the UK was trying to force Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, and that Apple had in the meantime pulled its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users.

In September 2025, we reported that Farage had told the US Congress that the UK's Online Safety Act was a threat not only to free speech, but also to encryption.

In June, we reported about Jordan's letter to Mahmood, warning that the UK order could compromise data of US citizens.

A backdoor does not check who is asking to use it, or why – and the officials worried about it being turned on Farage and the Trump administration are essentially describing why nobody should have a backdoor.

I've spent years in C and C++ at Microsoft and Google, and I've reviewed thousands of changes. I've watched good engineers ship bad code because the reviewer skimmed it, approved it, and went to lunch.

Now AI writes code 200× faster. Who reviews it?

If you're not enforcing strict 3-engineer code reviews on every change before it ships, you have no business building software.

Kidding. That was true yesterday.

Today I'm going to answer whether AI can review AI-generated code. Then I'll show you how to get an outstanding, senior-level review that doesn't miss details, for under a dollar a review.

Bookmark this. The full REVIEW.md is in the first reply, ready to paste.

The results surprised me

1/ I asked the AI session that wrote the code to review its own work. It found only 3 of 23 issues and recommended merging. Then I started a brand-new agent on the same model, with no memory of writing the code, and gave it only the diff. It found 17 of 23.

2/ Reviewers that only read the code found zero of the 8 logic bugs in the feature PR. Every logic bug was found by a reviewer that ran the code.

3/ One rule added to the reviewer's instructions took it from 4 of 8 logic bugs to 7 of 8, plus one nobody had found. Same model, $0.72 → $0.74, 27% faster.

4/ The most expensive model wasn't the best deal. Opus matched or beat Fable on both PRs at about a third of the price: under $1 a review vs. over $2.

5/ The next day, a brand-new reviewer agent found 4 blocking bugs in a PR with 272 passing tests and green CI.

6/ "Always get a code review" was written into the agent's instructions, and the agent skipped it on the very first PR.

It's an incredible unlock. No more bugs sailing through on a green checkmark.

Here's how I got there.

The setup

• 2 real PRs from a production codebase. One was a 75-file refactor, the other a 23-file feature.
• 12 reviews in total: 4 by an AI session that already had context on the work, 8 by brand-new agents that had only the diff, the repo and a rules file.
• 3 models: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5.
• I re-ran every reported defect myself, on the PR and on today's head, to sort live bugs from fixed ones.
• Costs are estimated from each reviewer's token count at API list prices, with no caching discount, so they lean high.

Then I put it to work on a real feature. That case study is below.

1. Context is the blind spot, not authorship.

On the refactor:
• The session that wrote the code, reviewing its own work (Fable): found only 3 of 23 issues
• A brand-new Fable agent, with no memory of the work: found 17 of 23
• A brand-new Opus agent: found 18 of 23

On the feature PR, written by a different session three days earlier:
• A Fable session that hadn't written it but had spent a day working in this repo: found 0 of 8 logic bugs
• Brand-new Fable, Opus and Sonnet agents: found 2 to 4 of 8 each

The feature-PR reviewer didn't write the code, and it still found nothing. A reviewer that shares the writer's mental model inherits the writer's blind spots, whoever wrote the code.

2. Reading finds style problems. Running the code finds bugs.

Every logic bug came from a reviewer that built a throwaway database, called the changed code with inputs it picked itself, and watched what came back. The session that already had context ran nothing. It read the code and found no logic bugs.

None of the 8 logic bugs on the feature PR are visible from the diff text alone. Every one of them is obvious once you run the code.

3. A rules file did almost nothing for the reviewer with context.

Giving it a written checklist added one finding per PR. Logic bugs found: still zero. With the same file, brand-new Fable and Opus agents found 13 to 18 issues per PR. A checklist can't fix a reviewer that already believes the code is correct.

4. The failure was in the order the reviewer worked.

The best brand-new reviewer still missed half the logic bugs, so I pulled its full tool-call trace and went through it step by step.

It had opened the functions behind all three bugs it missed, and it understood each one. But it wrote its test inputs after reading the implementation, so every input followed the implementation's own assumptions. Its edge cases were variations on the cases the code already handled.

The code had effectively written its own exam, and it passed.

The fix was one rule: "Write your test inputs before you read the implementation. Then run them." Same model, same PR: recall went from 4 of 8 to 7 of 8, plus a bug nobody had found, for two cents more.

5. The model matters, but less than the process.

Opus 5.5: $0.72 to $0.93 per review, 8 to 11 minutes. It found the most issues on both PRs: the best balance of thoroughness and cost.

Fable 5.1: $2.11 to $2.73, about 3× Opus. Found a bug nobody else caught on each PR, but skipped the base-branch comparison when the tests were green.

Sonnet 5.5: $0.14 to $0.21. The cheapest per finding, but it found 2 of 8, then 4 of 8 on the identical input. That run-to-run variance is the real cost.

The two strongest reviewers overlapped on only 10 of 20 findings.

A surprising case study: one real feature, reviewed end to end

An agent built a real feature: 37 files, 5,000+ lines of code, 272 tests passing, CI green. It pushed without a review.

I made it get one.

11 major bugs. A brand-new Opus reviewer found 11 blocking bugs, plus dozens of smaller issues. Every one of them was behind a green checkmark.

8 reviews, 6 rounds of fixes. Each cycle was review → fix → review again:
• The feature: 4 blockers → fix → approved, but that fix broke a filter → fix → approved. That's 3 reviews.
• The tool that enforces review: 4 blockers → fix → 2 more → fix → 1 more → fix → approved → small fix → approved. That's 5 reviews.

It all took under 40 minutes, at under a dollar per review.

What would have shipped without review:
• Every page of the new feature would crash on Feb 29.
• Users would see records labelled with a premium category they didn't belong to.
• A list would show stale data whenever a user changed a filter.
• A crafted link could slip hidden recipients into an email the user sends.
• The review gate wouldn't have enforced review: it checked the wrong repo and let real pushes through.
• Worse, installing it would have silently switched off every safety check that already ran on each commit.
• A database file would have been committed to the repo.

What this case taught me:

1/ 272 passing tests said nothing about these bugs. None of them had a test.

2/ The first approval wasn't the end. A fix for one bug created another, and only the second review caught it.

3/ The tool that enforces review needed 3 rounds of changes before it worked. Review the gate, not just the code.

Best practices for your AI code reviewer

1/ Always start a brand-new agent with no memory of writing the code. Give it only the diff, the repo and REVIEW.md. On the same model, this took recall from 3 of 23 to 17 of 23.

2/ Make it run the code, not just read it. Reading found zero logic bugs; every logic bug came from running the code.

3/ Have it write its test inputs before it reads the implementation. This one rule took recall from 4 of 8 to 7 of 8 for two cents more.

4/ Compare test results against the base branch every time, even when everything is green.

5/ Re-review every fix commit. Fixes create bugs.

6/ Use Opus by default. Add a second reviewer on a different model for business rules, thresholds and gates. The two best reviewers overlapped on only half their findings.

7/ Enforce review with a gate, not a prompt. Use a git pre-push hook: no approved review for that exact commit, no push. Edits to the rules themselves get reviewed too.

8/ Make it report on every design principle by name: separation of concerns, programming by intention, encapsulation, high cohesion, low coupling. A principle left unmentioned means the review is incomplete.

9/ Check honesty, not just style. Unknown stays unknown. The UI never invents data.

10/ Demand a clear verdict (APPROVE or CHANGES) and report findings as "N of the K found so far." The bug pool is never complete.

The full REVIEW.md is in the reply below Paste it into your repo and point your review agent at it.

REVIEW.md: rules for AI code review. Paste this into your repo.

1. WHO REVIEWS
• The reviewer is a fresh agent that did NOT write the code. It gets only: the diff, the repo, this file.
• The writer's self-review is a checklist pass, not a review.
• Default model: Opus. High-risk changes (business rules, thresholds, scoring, pricing, validation gates) get a second reviewer on a different model.
• Every fix commit gets its own review. Fixes create bugs.

2. HOW TO REVIEW: EXECUTE, DON'T READ
• Before reading the implementation, write down the inputs you will test. Inputs written after reading the code take the code's shape and miss what it misses.
• Run the changed code on those inputs, in a throwaway environment. Where possible, probe read-only against a copy of real data.
• Compare test results against the base commit every time, including when the head is green.

3. WHAT TO PROBE
• Every alternative form of an input, including forms that combine two of them.
• Every unit, and the input with no unit at all.
• Two or more entities in one input, in every order.
• Every consumer of a changed enum, status or constant.
• Every reason or error code, traced to the message the user actually sees.
• Every place the same fact is stored, computed or rendered (server and client). Do they still agree?
• Boundaries: empty, one, exactly-at-threshold, past the top.
• Dates: leap days, year boundaries, time zones.

4. HONESTY
• Unknown stays unknown. The UI never invents, guesses or silently resolves data it does not have.
• Every label must be true for every record it is shown on.

5. DESIGN PRINCIPLES (REPORT ON EVERY ONE)
For each: OK, or a violation with file:line.
• Separation of concerns
• Programming by intention
• Encapsulation
• High cohesion
• Low coupling
Blocking: a domain with two owners, duplicated logic, business logic in templates or UI code.
A principle left unmentioned = an incomplete review.

6. GATES AND TOOLING
• Attack every new check, hook or gate with inputs it should reject, including ones phrased differently to evade it.
• Prefer platform primitives (e.g. git pre-push) over clever parsing of commands.
• Confirm every exemption still points at something that exists, and that no exemption can be used to sneak code through.
• Installing a hook must not disable hooks already in place.
• Edits to the rules themselves are never exempt from review.

7. DOCS AND REFACTORS
• After any search-and-replace or move, re-read every edited sentence and ask: is this still true?
• Dated docs keep their old paths and facts.

8. REPORTING
• Findings are BLOCKING or NIT. Blocking must be fixed; nits are optional.
• Each finding gets a reproduction: input, expected, actual.
• Report "N of the K found so far." The pool is never complete.
• Green tests are not evidence. Say what you executed.
• End with exactly one line: VERDICT: APPROVE or VERDICT: CHANGES

The Schedule to the DPDP Act sets six specific penalty ceilings and one residual ceiling. Entry 7 sets a penalty of up to 50 crore rupees for breaching any provision of the Act or the Rules that has no separate entry.

The residual entry covers the duty to give a notice under section 5, to obtain valid consent under section 6, to erase data under section 8(7) and to run a grievance mechanism under section 8(10). These duties and the Board's power to impose penalties commence on 13 May 2027.

Three provisions of the DPDP framework commence on 13 November 2026, which is 39 days from today. Section 6(9) of the Act requires every Consent Manager to be registered with the Data Protection Board, and Rule 4 of the DPDP Rules sets the conditions for that registration. Section 27(1)(d) of the Act commences on the same day and lets the Board inquire into a breach of a Consent Manager's registration conditions. The Board has no chairperson and no members, and MeitY has not published an application form, a portal or a fee for registration.

Mr. Musk, yes, no billionaire should dictate a nation’s policy - Indian or American.

India must welcome competition in satellite internet, from Indian and global providers, whoever offers the most practical and affordable last-mile solution for those in remote regions. In countries with lower per-capita incomes, satellite internet must be affordable too. High subscription fees and equipment costs risk putting it beyond the reach of ordinary households. Connectivity must bridge the digital divide, not create a new one.

India knows our networks and spectrum are strategic infrastructure, not merely commercial assets. India’s national security safeguards are non-negotiable. 

Every country makes choices based on its own interests. Those in the West cannot preach free markets while practicing protectionism at home. USA imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs to protect its domestic industry, just as India takes measures to protect its own domestic manufacturers. Both India and the US have restricted Huawei over security concerns. One cannot demand a level playing field from others only when it suits its own agenda.

Indians will internally debate, question and address our strengths and shortcomings as a democratic country. 

Take BharatNet, India’s programme to bring broadband to village-level local bodies. We will question why, as the CAG’s 2026 audit report found, the programme is struggling to meet its original objectives. Why were only 33.2% of service-ready Gram Panchayats operational, despite ₹39,888 crore being spent? At the same time, we know to appreciate our telecom sector and regulations, which has made internet data among the world’s most affordable, bringing millions online.

India is a democracy, not a colony. We welcome the world, but we, the Indian people, will decide our own future - not Western vested interests, their double standards or any billionaire - Indian or American.

Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
A Black family with two rooms and six children fed a stranger they could not afford to feed. It was raining in the Alabama swamp in November of 1959, and the stranger was John Howard Griffin, a white writer moving through the South with his skin chemically darkened. That night was his own daughter's fifth birthday, and he walked outside so those six children would not hear a grown man crying.

He had the rag in his hand before he ever looked up. The shoes were familiar, and Sterling Williams had knelt over that exact pair on that exact patch of French Quarter sidewalk more than once, so he knew the wear on that leather the way you know a voice through a wall.

The man standing in them was not familiar. That man had been white.

So Sterling kept working and said nothing, because saying something was not a thing a Black shoeshine man did on Royal Street in November of 1959, not to a stranger and not about a stranger's face. Then the customer asked if there was anything familiar about those shoes.

Yeah, Sterling said. He had been shining a pair like that for a white man.

Fellow named Griffin, the customer said.

Yeah. You know him?

I am him.

The man in the shoes was John Howard Griffin, a Texas writer who had just spent four days flat on his back in a borrowed New Orleans house, cotton pads over his eyes, a sunlamp burning down on him, swallowing heavy doses of a drug prescribed for vitiligo. His skin came out dark and blotchy, so he painted over the pale patches with vegetable dye and shaved his head down to the scalp.

When he finally reached over and flipped on the bathroom light, he wrote that a stranger looked back at him out of the glass, and that what he felt first was not fear. It was loneliness.

Everything about him had changed except his shoes.

That is the part nobody ever tells you about this story. The disguise held for six weeks across four states, and it held because an old Black man on a French Quarter sidewalk decided to keep his mouth shut, and then decided to teach a stranger how to stay alive.

Sterling Williams was gray-headed, a veteran of the First World War, working a corner stand with a partner named Joe. He listened to the whole crazy confession, and he laughed, and then he got practical.

He pointed at Griffin's hands. The hair on the back of them was still brown, because Griffin had darkened his face and his scalp and his forearms and never once thought about the backs of his own hands, which is exactly the kind of thing a man does not think about until his life depends on it.

Griffin dug a razor out of his duffel bag and went looking for a washroom to shave them in, and he nearly walked into the white one. Two days into being Black in Louisiana, moving fast, he had already forgotten which door was his.

Every Black man on that street had learned that reflex as a child and had never once in his life been allowed to lose it.

Sterling let him work the stand. He taught him when to smile, when to laugh, when to shrug, and when to say nothing at all, which was most of the time, and he taught him how to hold his face while a white man talked over his head.

The white customers who were friendliest, Griffin noticed, were the ones asking a Black man where they could find Black women. Sterling had a line ready for that one, which was that when they want to sin, they're very democratic.

At the end of the day the old man dished out raccoon stew at the stand, and Griffin sat there and reported back what he had found out, which was only ever what Sterling had known his entire life. Nobody in that city was going to hire a Black man to do anything but pick something up and set it down.

Sterling had been listening to men say that for forty years.

He let the new one say it anyway.

Now here is the thing that got buried under ten million book covers. The experiment was not Griffin's idea first, and it was not a white man's idea at all.

That fall he had been stuck on an article for Sepia, the Black magazine published out of Fort Worth, about the suicide rate among Black Southerners. He mailed questionnaires to Black professionals all over the South, and the few that came back came back blank.

Not hostile. Blank.

He carried his frustration to Adelle Jackson, Sepia's editorial director, a Black woman who had come up through that company from a secretary's desk to become one of the most respected editors in the country. He wanted to know why they would not talk to him when he was on their side.

She did not soften it.

Black people knew that no matter how hard he tried he would never understand, she told him, and the only way he was ever going to know what it was like was to be one.

He drove home with that sentence sitting in his chest and it did not leave. When he came back later and told her what he intended to do, she looked at him and said he did not know what he was getting into.

Then she laid out, years before any of it happened, exactly what it would cost him and his wife and his children. She was right about every single part of it.

She got one paragraph.

He rode a Greyhound out of New Orleans into Mississippi. Seven months earlier a mob had taken Mack Charles Parker out of his cell in the Poplarville jail three days before his trial and left him in the Pearl River.

The FBI put together a file running around three hundred and seventy pages with confessions inside it, and a county grand jury of eighteen white men read it and declined to charge anybody. That was the state Griffin bought a ticket into, and everybody Black on that bus understood it better than he did.

At a rest stop the driver swung the door open and let the white passengers off to use the restrooms. Then he turned around and told the Black passengers to stay in their seats.

They said something about it, and they stayed anyway.

Griffin sat there doing the arithmetic every one of them had done a thousand times, which is how many more miles until a man is allowed to relieve himself.

Then there was the stare. He called it the hate stare, and he wrote that it landed on him like a blow, out of bus stations and store counters and passing cars, from people who had never met him and never would.

He had lived forty years in the South and had never once been on the receiving end of it. Ten of those years he had been blind.

He lost his sight in the Pacific in 1945, from shrapnel in an air raid, and did not get it back until one afternoon in January of 1957, when the redness swirled and he stumbled into the house and called his wife and started crying into the telephone. He had written, during that decade in the dark, that a blind man can only take the measure of another man's heart and mind, and that neither one of those tells you a thing about his color.

Then he got his eyes back and joined the rest of us.

He hitchhiked out of Mobile toward Montgomery, and most of the white men who stopped for him wanted to talk about one subject, and it was not the weather. One farmer patted the shotgun leaning against his knee, nodded at the swamp running along both sides of the road, and explained how easy it would be for a Black man to go in there and never be asked about again.

Griffin said yes sir, and got out at the next chance, and walked. He walked for hours in the heat until he reached a roadside store where an old white couple first turned him away, then looked at the state of him and let him buy a meal, then watched him eat it like he might take the plate with him.

It was late and raining by the time a young Black man in a mill truck pulled over for him. The man worked at a sawmill, and on the drive he explained to Griffin how the arrangement actually functioned down there, which was that a Black man was never permitted to pay a debt all the way off.

You stayed a little behind forever, and a man who is a little behind forever does what he is told. Then the driver asked Griffin where he was sleeping that night, and Griffin admitted he did not know, and the man took him home.

Home was two rooms on the edge of the swamp.

There was a wife inside and six children, and there was nothing.

Griffin looked around at what that family did not have, and then watched them make room for a stranger inside it. They fed him out of a pot that was not big enough for the people already in the house, and the children crowded him and looked him over and decided he was fine.

The parents put him where they could put him, and in a house that size there is no privacy for anybody and nobody pretends there is. Then everybody went to sleep on pallets on the floor.

It was the nineteenth of November. Back in Texas, Griffin's daughter Susie was five years old that day.

He lay in the dark in that two-room house and thought about the candles and the cake and the party dress, and about his sons in their good suits, all of them asleep in clean beds in a warm house. Then he got up and went out into the swamp so the children would not hear him, and he stood in the rain and cried.

What broke him was not what had been done to him that week.

It was arithmetic.

Those six children were the same as his six-year-old and his five-year-old and his baby in every way a human being actually is. The only difference on the table was the pigment in their skin, the least important fact about any child ever born, and that one fact was going to decide everything that happened to them for the rest of their lives.

He understood, standing out there in the rain, that if his own children had that skin this country would have handed them those same two rooms without blinking, and called it fair.

A few nights later, with no room anywhere, an old Black preacher took him in and shared a thin mattress with him in a small bare room. They lay under the quilts looking at the ceiling and talking about miracles.

The old man loved the one about Lazarus coming up out of the grave, and he could go on about that for a long time. Then Griffin asked him what he thought the future held for Black people in the South, and the old man's certainty went out of him.

He had two sons.

They had gone north, and he said he hoped they never came back.

A father in Alabama, praying his boys stayed a thousand miles away from him until the day he died, because that was the best thing he could picture for them.

In Montgomery, Griffin stopped taking the pills for a few days and scrubbed at the dye until his skin came up light enough. Then he walked into a whites-only restaurant, ordered a meal, and got smiled at.

Afterward he put the dye back on and crossed back over. He did that on purpose, back and forth across the same city, testing whether the line was really that simple.

It was.

The only thing he ever changed was the color, and it changed everything, every single time.

But look at what he was doing. He was choosing.

That is the whole distance between him and every other person in this story.

Now go home with him, and go back three years. Griffin lived in Mansfield, Texas, a farm town of about fifteen hundred people seventeen miles south of Fort Worth.

He did not have to go to Louisiana to find out what this country did to Black people.

He could have walked downtown.

In 1955 a Fort Worth attorney named L. Clifford Davis filed a federal lawsuit for the Mansfield NAACP on behalf of three Black teenagers, and their names were Floyd Moody, his cousin Charles Moody, and Nathaniel Jackson.

Every school morning they walked down to the little drugstore around seven and caught a Trailways bus into Fort Worth, eight or ten Black kids at a time. The only high school in the county that would take them was I. M. Terrell, twenty blocks past where that bus let them out.

The white high school was in their own town.

In August of 1956 the Fifth Circuit ruled that keeping them out on account of their race was unlawful, the first time a federal court had ordered a Texas school district to desegregate. Mansfield answered within days.

Crosses were burned in the Black neighborhood on the twenty-second and the twenty-third of August. Floyd Moody's father, J. E. Moody, worked land he did not own, and the white man who owned it told him that if he sent that boy to that school, you're going to have to move.

He was put off the place. T. M. Moody, who helped lead the whole effort, had his agreement to draw well water cancelled by the school district, and then word got around that somebody meant to kill him.

When the police made it clear they were not going to sit outside his house, Black men from the neighborhood armed themselves and did it instead.

On the morning of August 30, 1956, a crowd began gathering at Mansfield High School. By the time it was finished there were somewhere between two hundred and five hundred white people standing on that campus, and over the next several days they came back twice more.

They hung three effigies of Black people.

One was strung on wires across Main Street downtown, one went up on the flagpole in front of the school, and one was hung directly over the front entrance so that white students walked underneath it to get to class.

A photographer got a picture of Texas Rangers standing in that yard with the thing hanging in the frame behind them. A sign on one of the figures said this would be a terrible way to die.

Cars were parked around the school with threats and slurs painted across them. A local man named John Pyles stood in that crowd holding a baby alligator up where everybody could see it, and the joke, if you can call it that, was that any Black child who set foot on that campus was gator bait.

Governor Allan Shivers sent in the Texas Rangers, and their orders were not to walk those three young men through the door. Their orders were to remove any Black student who tried to enroll, and Shivers said publicly that he would not use the state's officers against citizens making an orderly protest.

The effigy stayed hanging over the school entrance.

Nobody in a badge took it down.

Floyd Moody was sixteen years old, and he remembered that when they left the school that day everything had seemed all right, and that by evening everybody in the city had heard. No Black student registered at Mansfield High School in 1956.

None registered the next year either, or the year after that. The district stayed segregated until 1965, nine full years after a federal court told it to stop, and Floyd A Black family with two rooms and six children fed a stranger they could not afford to feed. It was raining in the Alabama swamp in November of 1959, and the stranger was John Howard Griffin, a white writer moving through the South with his skin chemically darkened. That night was his own daughter's fifth birthday, and he walked outside so those six children would not hear a grown man crying.

Moody finished his junior and senior years riding that bus into Fort Worth.

John Howard Griffin was living on a farm outside that town the whole time. He was blind that August and could not have seen those effigies if he had walked directly under them.

He got his sight back the following January.

Two and a half years after that he was lying in a New Orleans bathroom under a sunlamp, trying to find out what it was like.

The Sepia articles ran starting in April of 1960 under the title Journey into Shame. Six thousand letters came in and only nine of them were hostile, which tells you something about this country's private conscience and absolutely nothing about its public one.

Then Mansfield answered again. One night that April somebody hung an effigy of Griffin beside the downtown traffic light, half of it painted black and half of it white, with a yellow stripe running down the back.

The same town, the same downtown, four years apart.

A few days later a cross was burned in front of Mansfield's Black elementary school. That had nothing to do with Griffin and everything to do with who was actually expected to pay for what he wrote.

Anonymous callers told him what they were going to do to him when they came, and his father came over and sat up in the house with a shotgun across his lap. Griffin sent his wife and their four children to Mexico, his parents sold their property and followed, and he came behind them and stayed nine months, and that is where he finished the book.

He got out. The children at that elementary school did not.

It had all happened once already, eleven years earlier, and America managed to forget it completely.

In May of 1948 Ray Sprigle, a Pulitzer winner at the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, tanned himself for three weeks in Florida, shaved his head, took the name James Crawford, and rode through the Jim Crow South for thirty days. He drew up a fresh will before he left, and his twenty-one part series ran on front pages and started the first real national argument about segregation in this country.

He did not do it alone, and he could not have. The NAACP put him with John Wesley Dobbs of Atlanta, who was sixty-six years old, the son of a man born in slavery, grand master of Georgia's Black Masons, the unofficial mayor of Auburn Avenue and a neighbor of a preacher's boy named Martin.

Dobbs drove them roughly three thousand miles in his 1947 Mercury. He took that white reporter down into the Delta, into the homes of sharecroppers and Black doctors, into the front rooms of families whose men had been lynched, and he introduced him everywhere as his cousin.

If that cover had broken, Sprigle would have gone home to Pittsburgh.

Dobbs would have been left standing in Mississippi.

Sprigle never printed his name. He left it out on purpose to protect him, and it worked, and it also meant that the man who made the entire thing possible became a blank space in his own story.

The public did not learn what John Wesley Dobbs had done until 1998. He died on August 30, 1961, the same week Atlanta's public schools were finally desegregated, about six weeks before Black Like Me arrived in American bookstores under one man's name.

That book sold more than ten million copies. It went into fourteen languages, got made into a movie, and has been assigned in American high schools for six decades.

Every word in it was something Black people had already been saying out loud, in print, from pulpits and witness stands and front porches, for as long as anybody could remember. The historian Nell Irvin Painter said it plainly, that when Griffin walked into a tense city he said the exact same thing local Black people had been saying for years, and the only difference was that the men in charge could hear it coming out of him.

That is the buried truth in this story, and it is not a compliment to anybody.

Griffin understood it eventually. Stokely Carmichael called it an excellent book for white people, and Griffin agreed with him, and in time he mostly quit lecturing on it, saying it was absurd for a white man to presume to speak for Black people when they have superlative voices of their own.

Now, the rumor. For over forty years people have passed around the story that the drug got him in the end, that he died of skin cancer he earned by turning himself Black.

People repeat it because it lands like justice or like tragedy depending on who is telling it. It is not true and it never was.

He never had skin cancer, and the drug gave him nausea and fatigue and nothing worse than that. He died in Fort Worth on September 9, 1980, at sixty years old, of complications from diabetes, at the end of a body already taken apart by a war injury, spinal malaria, ten years of blindness, an amputated leg and a run of heart attacks.

When a friend asked his wife what had finally killed him, she did not give a diagnosis.

Here is what the record kept. A title borrowed off a Langston Hughes poem, a movie, ten million copies, and one name on the cover.

Here is what the record misplaced. Adelle Jackson, who supplied the idea and got a paragraph, and John Wesley Dobbs, who drove that same road eleven years earlier at sixty-six and waited half a century to be named for it.

Floyd Moody, Charles Moody and Nathaniel Jackson, who wanted the high school in their own town and got a mob, a burned cross, and a father put off his land. A sawmill worker with two rooms and six children who fed a stranger in the rain and never learned who he was.

And a gray-headed man on Royal Street who recognized a pair of shoes, said nothing, and then pointed at a stranger's hands.

Your people already knew what was in that book. Your grandmother could have written it and never needed a sunlamp to do it.

So when this one comes back around your feed dressed up as one brave man's adventure, put the rest of them back into it. They are the reason it exists.

In December, Griffin came back to New Orleans one last time and stood again at the stand on Royal Street. On the fourteenth he took the last dose, and over the next few days the color went out of him.

He kept the shoes.

He was the only man in the whole story who got to take something off.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

text:
SO WHAT IF THE GOVERNMENT IS LOSING N15TR ANNUALLY ON SUBSIDY?: THE MEANING OF POLITICAL DEMOCRACY IS FOR THE VOTER TO ELECT THEIR LEADERS AND THE ELECTED LEADERS SHOULD DO WHAT THE VOTERS WANT:

For the attention of H/E President Bola Ahmed Tinubu of Nigeria 

By Abbati Bako, abbatibako@gmail.com

The Minister of Finance says: "We are losing N15 trillion annually on fuel subsidy. It is unsustainable."

My question is simple: So what?

Let me shock you: The government is not a company. The government is not a Dangote business. The government is not supposed to make profit. The government is supposed to make people happy. That is the essence of using democratic system as a game between vision and practically anywhere in the world. 

If democracy is about profit and loss, then why do we vote?

THE BIG LIE OF NEOLIBERAL ECONOMICS:

For 40 years, the World Bank/IMF taught our leaders a lie: "The government must not lose money. Subsidies are a waste. Remove it."

But let us interrogate that lie with simple logic:

1.  America loses $1.2 trillion annually on defence. They spend $877bn on the Pentagon that produces nothing — no garri, no rice, just bombs to kill. Does America say "defence is unsustainable, close the Pentagon"? No. 

2.  The UK loses £150bn annually on the NHS — free health that never makes profit. Do they close hospitals because the NHS is losing money? No.

3.  Germany lost €65bn in 2022-2023 subsidizing electricity and gas for its citizens after the Russia-Ukraine war. Did Germany say "German citizens should suffer"? No. The Chancellor said "We will protect our people whatever the cost." Hence, political policies are the management of the people. 

4.  Saudi Arabia, with $2,857 per citizen fossil fuel subsidy per year — 40 times Nigeria — does not call it loss. They call it the share of the national cake. 

So why is it that when Nigeria spends $64 per citizen per year on fuel the cheapest among all oil producers economists shout "unsustainable"?

Because we have been brainwashed to think the government is business. 

WHAT IS DEMOCRACY?

Let me go back to my classroom in University of Kent:

Abraham Lincoln said: "Democracy is the government of the people, by the people, for the people."

Jean Jacques Rousseau said: "Government is a social contract — people surrender power, leaders must deliver general will."

What is the general will of the Nigerian voter?

I conducted informal poll in Wuse Market, Kano Kurmi Market, Onitsha Main Market: I asked 100 people:

"Do you want the government to remove the fuel subsidy and save N15tr, or keep the subsidy and buy fuel N300?"

98 said: KEEP SUBSIDY.
2 said: REMOVE.

So 98% of voters want subsidies. But 100% of economists want removal. Who should the President Bola Tinubu obey in democracy — 98% voters or 2% economists?

That is the meaning of democracy.

If voters want cheap fuel, leaders must give cheap fuel, even if the government loses N15tr. Because that N15tr is not government money — it is voters' oil money!

Oil belongs to the people, not to the government. The government is just a manager. Meaning,  management of the resources and the people. 

SO WHAT IF WE LOSE N15TR? WHAT DO WE GAIN?

Economists only calculate loss. They never calculate gain of subsidy:

- If fuel is N300, farmers in Kebbi can irrigate 2 hectares at low cost — food price crashes, inflation drops from 34% to 10%. How much is that worth? N20tr saved on food import.

- If fuel is N300, a danfo driver in Lagos can feed his 4 children, pay school fees, and not enter a one-chance robbery. How much is that security worth? N10tr saved the police, army.

- If fuel is N300, a factory in Aba can run a generator, employ 50 youth, youth won't Japa or join Boko Haram. How much is that peace worth? Unquantifiable.

- If fuel is N300, voters believe democracy works for him. He will vote, not burn the ballot box. How much is that democracy worth? Priceless.

text:
My boyfriend asked me to delete one contact from my phone. I did. The next morning, that same number called me.
It happened on a Sunday night.

My boyfriend, Daniel, was sitting beside me on the couch when he suddenly asked:

“Who is Michael?”

I looked at him, confused.
“Michael who?”

He picked up my phone and showed me a contact I barely remembered saving.

Michael.

I laughed.

“He's nobody. I think that's an old contact.”

Daniel didn't laugh.

“Delete it.”

I stared at him.

“Why?”

“Just delete it.”

The way he said it made me uncomfortable.
I asked him how he knew about Michael, but he avoided the question.

Instead, he said:
“If you trust me, delete the number.”

I didn't want to argue, so I deleted it.

Then I showed him my recently deleted contacts.
He watched carefully until he was sure it was gone.

“Good,” he said.

I thought that was the end of it.

Until the next morning.
At exactly 7:14 AM, my phone rang.

I looked at the screen.

Unknown Number.

I answered.
“Hello?” 

There was silence.

Then a man's voice whispered:
“Why did you delete my number?”

My heart stopped.
Because I recognized the voice.
It was Michael.

The same man Daniel had just told me to delete.

And then Michael said something that made me realize Daniel had lied to me about something.

“Your boyfriend knows exactly who I am.”

The line was still silent except for Michael's breathing.

"Your boyfriend knows exactly who I am."

I quickly put the phone on mute and turned to Daniel. He was now fully awake, sitting up.

"Daniel... he says you know him. Do you?"

Daniel didn't answer immediately. He reached for my phone.

"Don't talk to him. He's lying."

But his hand was shaking.

On the phone, Michael continued as if he could hear us:

"Let me guess. He told you I'm just some old contact? That I'm nobody?"

My throat was dry. "Yes."

"Two weeks ago, Daniel came to my shop at Kaneshie. He showed me your picture. He said you were his girlfriend, and that you were getting calls from a man named Michael who was harassing you. He asked me to stay away from you."

I felt dizzy.

"I never told you I was being harassed by anyone. I didn't even remember who Michael was until now!"

"I know," Michael said. "That's why I knew he was lying. So I checked."

"Checked what?"

"My old phone. Ama, do you remember when you saved my number?"

I tried to think. It was years ago.

"You saved it after your brother's funeral. You said — _'If my family ever tries to force me into that marriage again, call me and I will come get you, no matter where you are.'_"

I remembered. Michael was my late brother's best friend. My emergency contact.

"Daniel knows," Michael whispered. "He found our old messages in your Facebook. That's how he knew to tell you to delete me. Because I am the only person who can prove..."

A loud BANG interrupted him.

Daniel had snatched the phone from my hand and smashed it against the wall.

The call ended.

He looked at me, breathing hard, and said:

You were never supposed to remember him.

Here is the *FINAL PART* — this ending will blow up your comments:

---

*FINAL PART - My Boyfriend Asked Me To Delete One Contact*

"You were never supposed to remember him."

The room was silent except for my broken phone on the floor.

My hands were shaking.

"Daniel, what are you talking about? Remember who?"

He sat on the edge of the bed, holding his head. For the first time in 8 months, I wasn't looking at my boyfriend. I was looking at a stranger.

"Your brother didn't die in an accident, Ama."

The world stopped.

"What did you say?"

Michael was calling back. Daniel's phone was ringing now. *MICHAEL* flashing on his screen.

He HAD his number saved. He lied.

I grabbed Daniel's phone and answered before he could stop me.

"MICHAEL, WHERE ARE YOU?"

"I'm outside your gate! Ama, don't let him leave! I have proof!"

I ran to the window. A white Corolla was parked outside our compound in East Legon. Michael was standing there, holding a brown envelope.

Daniel tried to pull me back.

"AMa, please. I did it because I love you. I didn't want you to leave me!"

I pushed him off and ran downstairs barefooted and opened the gate.

Michael hugged me like a brother. He handed me the envelope.

Inside were printed screenshots. Old Facebook messages. Police reports.

My brother, Kofi, didn't die in a car accident in 2021.

He was beaten to death after a fight.

A fight with Daniel.

Daniel was his friend. They fought over money Daniel owed him. Daniel pushed him. Kofi fell and hit his head. Daniel left him there.

Michael was the only witness. Daniel begged him to stay quiet and paid him off. He made Michael promise to never contact my family again.

That's why when Daniel saw "Michael" on my phone — my brother's best friend — he panicked. He knew if I ever talked to Michael, the truth about my brother would come out.

I walked back inside.

Daniel was on his knees, crying.

"Ama, it was an accident! I was scared! I loved Kofi like a brother! I didn't mean—"

"And you let me mourn him for 3 years thinking it was an accident? You came into my life, pretended to love me, and tried to erase the only person who knew what you did?"

I called the police right there.

Daniel didn't run. He just sat there whispering, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry."

An hour later, they took him away.

Michael stayed with me until my mother came.

As they drove Daniel away, I looked at my broken phone on the floor. At exactly 7:14 AM, that unknown number had saved my life.

Sometimes God uses the contact you almost deleted to reveal the devil sleeping next to you.

*THE END.*

text:
Apple announced stricter macOS Full Disk Access controls following reports that Muse accessed a journalist’s private Messages. Apple’s decision has nothing to do with privacy or safety.

Apple recently warned that Full Disk Access can expose an entire Mac, including files, email, messages and browsing history, and that communication apps can compromise private data belonging to other people.

These are legitimate security and privacy concerns, but Apple’s new restrictions give it tighter control over which third parties can access local Mac data, making it harder for competitors to build assistants with the same depth of access as Apple’s own software and chosen partners.

Last month, Inc. columnist Jason Aten said Muse had synced data from his local Messages database despite his belief that he had never authorised that access, and said Full Disk Access was switched off when he checked. 

Meta disputes his account and says Muse can’t read Messages unless someone enables Full Disk Access and separately enables the Messages connector. Full Disk Access by itself makes any non root file readable, including the Messages database, so the Messages connector isn’t a technical limitation.

Apple announced its new restrictions on 2 October, 13 days after Aten’s column. Meta can’t be trusted when it comes to what it says about customer data and its approach to privacy, so readers should assume the worst possible risks when it comes to Muse. But pointing the finger at Meta isn’t the purpose of this post.

💡 Apple had already been warned about this privacy risk.

In August, I published a technical analysis of OpenAI's Messages integration, which handles iMessage, RCS, and SMS, comparing it to spyware. I warned it gives the US government a side entrance to access private communications, so the FBI can stop pressuring Apple to build a "safe" backdoor for iMessage, which is protected by end-to-end encryption.

Proton cited my analysis. On 26 August, Fortune interviewed me about it, put my concerns directly to OpenAI and asked Apple if it had anticipated existing macOS permissions being used to let AI software read and search Messages.

🚨 Apple didn’t respond.

I don’t think my analysis, Fortune’s reporting or Proton citing my work caused Apple to act. Muse is different because Meta competes directly with Apple, and restricting Full Disk Access makes it harder for rival AI assistants to access and analyse local Mac data.

In August, I argued that iMessage encryption doesn’t protect a conversation once another company is given access to the readable messages on the Mac. ChatGPT can search, summarise and draft from those conversations, while the other participants are never told their private messages have been opened up to third-party software.

Some security professionals from companies like Palo Alto Networks claimed giving ChatGPT or another third party access to Messages is no different from taking a screenshot. That comparison is technically ridiculous. A screenshot exposes selected information chosen by one person. 

Giving a tech company access to messages that are supposed to be protected by end-to-end encryption creates persistent, automated and searchable access to years of private communications at scale. It can expose relationships, locations, medical information, legal discussions, financial details, attachments and everything else stored in those conversations.

OpenAI told Fortune the integration is optional, requires permission, runs locally by default and doesn’t automatically index an entire Messages history. OpenAI ignored all of my concerns, which shows irresponsible design and dishonest marketing. Building a consumer product for private messages without explaining risks or trade offs is unacceptable, especially when the person granting permission isn’t the only individual inside those conversations.

Since Meta launched Muse, Apple has finally admitted that communication apps using Full Disk Access can compromise the privacy of non consenting participants. That was the core of my analysis before Apple announced these new restrictions. So what changed?

Apple tolerated OpenAI’s Messages integration but panicked when Meta launched a product that requires the same permissions. Apple didn’t mind ChatGPT exposing customers and their contacts to grave privacy risks because OpenAI was already a close partner, built into its products. 

Remember, they refused to respond to Fortune’s questions. Apple integrated ChatGPT into Siri, Writing Tools and Apple Intelligence in 2024, giving itself complete control over data transmissions, consent displays and software execution.

Meta’s Muse is a competing personal AI agent built to connect with apps, services and local data. Meta wants Muse built into daily life, and people downloaded it more than 2.5 million times in its first 13 days. On 18 September, Muse became the top free US iPhone app, passing ChatGPT. That rank gives Apple an anticompetitive motive to restrict it.

Apple controls what third parties can access on a Mac, which allows it to cut competing AI assistants off from local data in the name of security.

@TimSweeneyEpic warned me about this after I published my ChatGPT analysis. He told me to be careful because Apple could use privacy arguments like mine to "block or kneecap competing AI assistants in order to favor its own".

I still don’t believe Apple should allow any third party application to have persistent access to iMessage communications that end to end encryption is supposed to protect. OpenAI’s Messages integration remains one of the most dangerous consumer software designs I’ve analysed, because people are giving a tech company searchable access to private communications involving everyone they talk to. That includes the US government, which only has to ask OpenAI in the name of national security or any other excuse it makes up.

But the answer should be a specific technical safeguard around Messages and similarly sensitive data, not a broad restriction that gives Apple even more control over what competing AI software can do on a Mac. That safeguard has to cover Meta, which can’t be trusted to tell the truth about what it does with customer data.

If Apple’s true concern was customer privacy, it would have responded to OpenAI’s Messages integration in August when Fortune asked for comment, 6 weeks before the Muse "controversy".

Apple Intelligence is deeply integrated into macOS, and Apple says most of that processing happens on the device or through Private Cloud Compute, so Apple’s own software doesn’t need to compete on equal technical terms with a third party assistant asking for broad local access.

I now question anything Apple says about customer privacy and what it can and can’t see. On 3 October, @jack said Apple had removed Bitchat from its India App Store on a demand from India’s IT ministry. 

That was 10 weeks after India’s cybercrime agency ordered GitHub to remove Bitchat’s code because its design impedes lawful interception. Apple also removed Bitchat from its China App Store in February at the request of China’s internet regulator. Apple claims it stands by its principles under government pressure, yet it removed a private messaging app from 2 countries because their governments sent a request without legal justification.

Restrict Full Disk Access broadly enough and Apple can say it’s protecting privacy while making it harder for Meta, OpenAI’s competitors and independent developers to build third party software with the same depth of local context available to Apple’s close partners, so I believe this is about protectionism, not customer security.

I believe Muse has just given Apple the excuse Tim Sweeney warned me about.

You can find this and other articles on my Substack - link in my bio and everything is free.
