Protest by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Protest : Long & short term steps necessary

It refers to protest by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar (New Delhi) subsequently shifted first outside Parliament House and then outside Sewa Tirth (Pradhan Mantri Residence) on 21.07.2026. Media Reports including on social media indicate that divided opposition has got itself “employed” against national interest in infiltrating the protest initially started by students of a particular ideology with getting Sonam Wangchuk.

If resignation of concerned minister is solution to the problem, then perhaps practically ultimately one by one all the ministers will have to resign in a country having population of more than 140 crore persons. Undoubtedly paper-leak is a very big problem for affected students, and precautionary steps need to be taken to stop the menace. So called students’ agitation on the matter is being fuelled with active role of several foreign-funded Non-Government-Organisations (NGOs) and political leaders with really affected students being mute spectator to all such happenings. These elements are present ever where in such situations like so-termed Farmers’ Agitation.

With so many police-men injured including senior ones Special Commission, Joint Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner and assistant Commissioner of Delhi Police badly injured and many police-vehicles broken and pubic-property damaged, it has become necessary to take some harsh steps against the hooligans to maintain morale of police-force.

It was in past when India had a very small population as compared to present, that the then Railway Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned from his post following a rail-accident.  But that cannot be possible with country’s population having risen manifolds.

It is beyond understanding why and how Central Government is giving so much importance to the issue when liberal approach of Central Government in sending the minister and other senior ones to opposition leaders to find some solution was later turned down by the senior opposition leaders. It is time to take some strong steps by the central government to ensure proper governance and smooth running of Parliament.

What India needs a politics of cordiality amongst ruling party and main opposition party like was in days when PV Narsimharao was Prime Minister and Atal Bihari Vajpayee was the Opposition Leader. It may be recalled that the then Prime Minister PV Narsimharao trusted the ever trustworthy Atal Bihari Vajpayee who was at that time Leader of opposition (LoP) to go to Geneva in 1994 to lead the Indian delegation at the United Nations Human Rights Commission (UNHRC) meeting, perhaps only occasion in the history of Universe.

Sometimes change of name also results in tackling the problems. For example, Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi has become an institution to carry on anti-national activities by students of a particular ideology who continue to enjoy almost free-of-cost facility of boarding and lodging in the capital city of India without any aim to take study seriously. Same is situation at Aligarh Muslim University at Aligarh (UP). Both these Universities need name-change like Dr Sarvpalli Radhakrishnan University and Dr APJ Abdul Kalam University respectively.

What India needs is drastic and important poll-reforms to achieve the goal that trough an ordinance without waiting for some never to-be-achieved political consensus. Simultaneous elections to Lok Sabha and state-assemblies should be three-tier with elections to municipal bodies also included in the ideal system. Elections to posts of President and the Vice President may be held simultaneously by all MPs and MLAs in the manner President is elected but through EVMs equipped with VVPAT on nominations signed by at least 34-percent MPs to ensure direct elections. In case of vacancy caused at post of President, Vice President may be made President for rest of the term. But in case of vacancy caused at post of Vice President, an interim Vice President may be elected by MPs only for rest of the term. However, in case both regularly elected President and Vice President may not be on post, fresh simultaneous elections for both the posts should be held without waiting for five-years period.

Prime Minister/Chief Ministers with Speakers and Deputy Speakers of the lower Houses should be elected through secret and compulsory vote of members of the Lower Houses through Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) equipped with VVPAT on nominations signed by at least 34-percent members. Such an elected Prime Minister/Chief Minister may be removed by same process but with compulsion of naming alternate leader in the same motion. Members not opting to vote may lose voting-right in the House even though retaining membership of the House. Without adopting such a system, aspect “One-Nation One-Election” can never be a dream-cum-true because of mid-term elections caused due to hung Lok Sabha/state-assembly or fall of governments in between. Even present Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, Speakers and Deputy Speakers may be re-elected on lines suggested here-above. Since a person cannot represent two constituencies or become member of both Parliament and state-assembly, no person should be allowed to contest from more than one constituency or for both Parliament and state-assembly. A sitting MP or MLA should resign first from his/her earlier seat before filing nomination for the other seat. Membership of a Parliamentarian must be auto-terminated on taking oath in a state as minister (or Chief Minister) and vice-versa to prevent situation like Atal Bihari Vajpayee government falling due to single controversial vote of the then Odisha Chief Minister Girdhar Gomango who did not resign from Lok Sabha even becomin Odisha Chief Minister. 

Secret voting for Rajya Sabha elections should be restored but through EVMs equipped with VVPAT system with simultaneous elections for full time and part time members. Persons getting more votes should be declared elected for full terms, and those with successive less votes may be declared elected for part terms. Constitution should be amended to abolish useless provision of Legislative Councils which is practically for political assignment to favourites and relations of political leaders. Only those not having contested any election in life should be appointed nominated members of Rajya Sabha. No MP or MLA should retain any type of post in their party or even in society. Ministerial-strength should be reduced for 10-percent of strength of lower House. Post of Parliamentary Secretaries should be abolished.

Security-losing persons should be barred from contesting elections for next six years. ‘None-of-the-above’ (NOTA) option should be made practically useful. All candidates getting votes less than ‘NOTA’ may be barred from contesting any future election even though in case NOTA winning in any constituency, next to NOTA may be declared elected but only for that term. Thereafter he may lose right to contest any election in life-time.

There must be at least some minimum educational qualification to contest any elections. Best is to constitute an “Indian Political Service” on lines of “Indian Administrative Service (IAS)”. It is ridiculous that so well-educated officers from IAS and allied services are at times ruled by uneducated political leaders. System will automatically abolish faulty practice of family-politics where politicians often misuse politics like some family-business rather than a tool for service to the people. Case of George Fernandez elected to Rajya Sabha despite having lost all his memory, even calls for medical-fitness certificates before allowing contesting elections.

Absconding Parliamentarian from court-summons/warrants if present at Sansad Bhawan even for attending the session, should not be allowed to leave Sansad Bhawan till police-authorities reach for execution of warrants. Parliamentarians and legislatures with attendance less than say 75-percent in the House should not be allowed to contest any elections for next six years. Immunity to elected representatives should be withdrawn even from legislative proceedings because in the infamous JMM-bribery case even the Apex Court expressed its inability to act against guilty ones because their bribed act to vote for Narsimharao-government was considered to be immunised being under Parliamentary proceedings. Rules of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha should be re-written in a stringent manner by encoding fixed punishments for Parliamentarians for not following rules and norms, snatching discretionary powers of Chairpersons and Parliamentary committees. Lok Sabha mildly punished its member Rajesh Manjhi taking his lady-friend as his wife on foreign-trip at government-expense by just barring him from few sittings of Lok Sabha even though such an act was not even immunised under Parliamentary proceedings.

Parliamentarians should be required to compulsory fill all their particulars in their bio-data including details of their assets, name of spouse/s etc to be put on public domain of websites of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. This can check several malpractices like hiding name of additional (more than one spouse) like was done by Dharmendra when he did not disclose name of Hema Malini also as his wife.

Rule should be to make all deductions of government-dues like of water, electricity, telephone, rent or any other from salary/perks/pensions etc payable to them. Pensions should be hold till former Parliamentarians/Ministers do not vacate government-accommodations. Defaulters should be barred from contesting any next elections till all dues are cleared against them, and non-entitled government-accommodations are vacatedEither the Prime Minister or political party sponsoring that Prime Minister may deposit advance-money for use of IAF aircrafts for non-official use.

Since political parties are not complying with CIC-verdict bringing these under purview of RTI Act, all direct/indirect government-funding including tax-exemptions, subsidized land or leased government-accommodations, free voters’ list and free Doordarshan/ Radio timings etc should be abolished. Political parties not having contested any election in last five years should be de-recognised. Sections 13A, 80GGB and 80GGC of Income Tax Act on contributions received-by and made-to political parties should be totally abolished to prevent whitening of black money by political parties getting themselves registered but not contesting elections. Live TV-debates between prominent leaders and Prime-Ministerial/Chief-Ministerial candidates should replace mega-budgeted rallies and road-shows which should be rather banned. Corruption-generating MPLADS should be abolished. Pensions to MPs and MLAs have no logic when it has been done away with government-servants. Persons with more than two children should not be allowed to contest elections. To avoid life-long ambitions of politicians to remain in power, there may be an upper age-limit of say 65 years to contest direct elections. Experienced persons if needed in the ministry can be elected as Rajya Sabha members. Retired judges of Supreme Court and High Courts must not be given post-retirement assignments or allowed to be in politics for two years after their retirement from judiciary, or else they may lose all their post-retirement benefits or appointment as arbitrators.

WHEN A SENIOR ADVOCATE SAYS HE HAS LOST HOPE IN THE SUPREME COURT, INDIA MUST LISTEN. ⚖️💔

READ THE REPORTS:

LiveLaw: https://t.co/TbYlz3VoP9

Moneycontrol: https://t.co/Xmi3IthZ0l

India Today: https://t.co/f952Ge7jSu

The Economic Times: https://t.co/f7Wm1F1rHy

“I am tired of keeping on going to the Supreme Court. I am speaking for myself. I don't think there is any use of going there. I don't have much hope in the Supreme Court of India.”

These are deeply troubling words from Kapil Sibal, a senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP, expressing his personal frustration with repeatedly approaching the highest court for relief.

His remarks followed the police restrictions and detentions surrounding the 10 October protests in Delhi over alleged electoral-roll irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process.

This is bigger than one lawyer's disappointment. It raises fundamental questions about access to justice, the protection of voting rights and the responsibility of constitutional institutions to safeguard citizens' freedoms.

🗳️ WHEN VOTING RIGHTS ARE IN QUESTION, SILENCE IS NOT AN ANSWER

Sibal raised concerns about alleged wrongful deletions and inclusions in electoral rolls, arguing that repeated appeals to the courts had not produced the relief he expected. These are serious concerns that deserve transparent scrutiny. The underlying records and the circumstances of individual cases must be examined before sweeping conclusions are drawn.

Every eligible citizen must have a fair opportunity to vote. If wrongful exclusion is established, timely corrective action and accountability are essential. No administrative process should leave eligible voters struggling to establish a right guaranteed by the Constitution.

⚖️ THE SUPREME COURT MUST REMAIN A BEACON OF JUSTICE

The Supreme Court is not merely another government institution. Its constitutional role includes protecting fundamental rights, reviewing state action and ensuring that public power remains within the limits of the law.

Criticism of judicial decisions is not an attack on the Constitution. In a democracy, institutions must be open to reasoned scrutiny—especially when citizens believe their rights are at stake.

Public confidence requires reasoned judgments, accessible remedies, consistent application of the law and meaningful relief when rights have been violated.

🚨 PEACEFUL PROTEST IS A DEMOCRATIC RIGHT

Sibal also questioned restrictions surrounding the Delhi protest and raised concerns about the detention of people seeking to participate.

Authorities may impose lawful, proportionate restrictions where genuinely necessary to protect public order and safety. But restrictions must have a legal basis, and detentions must follow due process. Peaceful dissent must not be treated as a threat merely because it challenges those in power.

The right to protest, freedom of expression and the right to vote are not favours granted by the government. They are essential elements of a constitutional democracy.

🇮🇳 INDIA NEEDS ACCOUNTABILITY—AND A JUSTICE SYSTEM THAT INSPIRES HOPE

Sibal's statement reflects his personal loss of confidence; it does not, by itself, prove that the entire judiciary has failed. But it should prompt serious public discussion about whether citizens are receiving timely, effective remedies when they allege violations of their rights.

The answer cannot be to abandon the courts. It must be to strengthen judicial independence, improve access to justice, examine credible allegations impartially and ensure that constitutional protections work in practice—not merely on paper.

A DEMOCRACY IS TESTED NOT BY HOW COMFORTABLY IT TREATS THE POWERFUL, BUT BY HOW FAITHFULLY IT PROTECTS THE RIGHTS OF ORDINARY CITIZENS.

When voting rights are questioned, peaceful protesters are detained and experienced advocates express despair about obtaining relief, democratic institutions must respond with transparency, constitutional fidelity and justice.

THE CONSTITUTION MUST BE MORE THAN A PROMISE. JUSTICE MUST BE MORE THAN A HOPE.

Open Letter to Elon Musk: Who Controls the Signal?
Sovereignty, Selective Outrage, and the Real Costs of Private Connectivity

Dear @ElonMusk,

Things are rarely pure coincidence when timing, platforms, and pressure align against a state’s control of its own communications and industrial backbone. Toolkits, timed reports, selective outrage, and spontaneous amplification on the same platforms have long been used to loosen sovereign oversight of critical infrastructure. When a private operator holds the ability to enable, restrict, or reroute connectivity above national borders, the stakes move from market access to national security. Democracies worldwide face the same question. Who decides when the signal stays on, and under whose law?

Your recent posts on India illustrate the pattern. The sequence began with references to "unnamed oligarchs" maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian people. It moved to a direct question asking whether Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss" of India. It continued with a sarcastic address to "Prime Minister Ambani" suggesting monopolistic exploitation. 

India’s Ministry of Communications has stated that its satellite communications framework is fair and non-discriminatory. Three licensees, including Starlink, remain at comparable stages pending security clearances from the Home Ministry and spectrum assignment. Starlink received its GMPCS licence and IN-SPACe approval earlier. Final security conditions, including lawful interception, data routing through Indian gateways, and local storage requirements, remain outstanding. These rules trace in part to the 2008 Mumbai attacks, in which satellite phones were used by the perpetrators. Regulatory caution is not new. Framing a security process as personal capture of the economy is.

Certain profiles receive selective amplification in these sequences. Engagement with disgruntled voices inside India, including responses that welcome the outsider and gesture toward further targets, fits a broader pattern of treating regulatory caution as evidence of capture. Some amplify the charge while remaining silent on identical restrictions applied by other states and on the documented dual-use record.

Your selective silence is notable. Mainland China has never licensed Starlink. Terminals are prohibited equipment. Traffic does not route through Chinese gateways. Beijing treats the constellation as a dual-use national security concern because of foreign control and potential military application. Your substantial Tesla operations in China have not produced equivalent public campaigns against that ban. The same contrast appears with Huawei, ZTE, and TikTok. The United States and multiple allies restricted or banned those systems on documented grounds of equipment risk, data access by foreign governments, and dual-use potential. National security arguments are applied rigorously against some foreign networks and treated as obstacles when applied to others.

Documented criminal adaptation supplies concrete evidence of the risk. In November 2024, Indian authorities intercepted a Myanmarese trawler near Barren Island carrying approximately 6,000 kilograms of methamphetamine. A Starlink Mini terminal was recovered. Investigators stated the smugglers used it for navigation and encrypted messaging with Golden Triangle handlers. In July 2025 the Colombian Navy seized an unmanned semi-submersible equipped with a Starlink antenna and linked to the Gulf Clan, assessed as a test for remote cocaine transport. Similar terminals have been documented at illegal gold mining sites in Brazil’s Amazon, leading authorities to require identification for new users in the region. In Myanmar, Starlink terminals powered scam compounds involved in human trafficking and cyber-fraud. SpaceX has stated it disabled more than 2,500 kits near suspected centers. Nigerian troops have reported intercepting hundreds of devices allegedly used by Boko Haram and ISWAP. These are reported seizures and operational adaptations spanning 2024 to 2026.

The Ukraine case remains the clearest demonstration of private control over a sovereign military operation. After the 2022 Viasat disruption, Starlink became essential for Ukrainian communications. In September 2022 Ukrainian forces sought coverage near Sevastopol for a maritime drone operation against the Russian Black Sea Fleet. You declined, stating that enabling it would make SpaceX explicitly complicit in a major act of war. Coverage over Crimea had not been active. The request was refused. Ukrainian drones lost their link. The episode showed that a single private decision determined the reach of a military action by a country at war. Russian forces have since used smuggled terminals to extend drone ranges. SpaceX has worked with Ukrainian authorities to geofence some misuse. The dependency and the discretion both exist.

A parallel form of external pressure has targeted large indigenous industrial groups. The Adani Group is one of India’s largest infrastructure conglomerates, with major positions in ports, airports, power, and logistics. In January 2023, Hindenburg Research published a report accusing the group of stock manipulation and opaque offshore structures, describing it as the largest con in corporate history. Adani denied the claims. Within days listed stocks lost more than $100 billion in market value at the lowest point. A major public offering was cancelled. Indian reporting later described the group’s response as "Operation Zeppelin", combining legal, cyber, and investigative efforts, with noted collaboration with Israeli-linked intermediaries. The report appeared days before Adani was set to close a $1.2 billion deal for a stake in Israel’s Haifa port. Hindenburg Research closed operations in January 2025. Adani stocks later recovered a substantial portion of the lost value. The short-term damage to valuations and project timelines was nonetheless measurable. Were it not for the deep ties and collaboration between India and Israel, this major risk might never have been thwarted.

The pattern of external reports timed against strategic industrial groups appears in other Global South markets. In 2023 Hindenburg published a report on Nigeria-focused Tingo Group, a Nasdaq-listed agri-fintech company, calling the business an exceptionally obvious scam. Tingo’s shares fell more than 50 percent in a single session. The company disputed the claims. Similar short reports have targeted other cross-listed emerging-market firms. In each case selling pressure and delayed capital raises hit companies whose primary operations sit outside deep Western capital markets. For infrastructure-heavy groups the result can be slower expansion of ports, energy capacity, or connectivity that governments treat as national priorities.

These patterns carry implications for democracies everywhere. Low-Earth-orbit systems bypass terrestrial gateways that states traditionally use for lawful interception, data residency, and emergency control. A private operator can apply geographic limits or refuse extensions based on its own judgment. External research reports can erase billions in market value in days. Gray markets move hardware faster than regulation. Countries that restricted Huawei or similar equipment did so because foreign control of critical communications creates leverage during crisis. The same logic applies when the operator is commercial. Bolivia moved from years of refusal on sovereignty grounds to rapid licensing after a change in government. Other nations have gone further, filing complaints with the ITU over unauthorized transmissions into their territory. Multiple states continue to require local gateways and security clearances before commercial service. These are responses to observed dual-use and criminal diversion.

Pressure campaigns that treat security clearances as corruption, amplify selective free-speech claims, and ignore identical restrictions elsewhere follow a recognizable sequence. Connectivity benefits are real in remote areas and disaster zones. So are the documented uses by cartels and non-state groups, the demonstrated ability of one company to decide coverage in an active conflict, and the measurable economic cost of sudden valuation shocks to indigenous industrial capacity. 

Democracies that value both open information and sovereign control of critical infrastructure face the same tension. Consistency in applying national security standards would strengthen rather than weaken the case for expanding access. The pattern is visible to those who compare the cases rather than the slogans. 

Eyes open. Dates and decisions still matter.

Respectfully,

Concerned observers of democracy, digital rights, and sovereignty

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Dear @elonmusk ,
Since 59 million people read your letter, a few facts.
And before I start, a bit about me. I am a mere yoga practitioner. So India is not for beginners like you eliciting a response from my leader. I am enough. 

Now the response. 

Starlink is not "unlicensed." 

DoT granted your licence in June 2025. IN-SPACe authorised your constellation in July 2025. 
What is pending is commercial spectrum and final security clearance, and Jio's own satellite venture and OneWeb are waiting in the same queue, under the same rules. 

If Ambani were the "real boss of India," his company wouldn't be standing in line behind the Cabinet with yours.

On the one question you actually fought him on, auction versus administrative allocation, India sided with you. Jio then signed up to sell your kits. Strange behaviour for a monopolist supposedly blocking you.

Why the caution? 

Starlink terminals have been reported in the hands of smugglers and insurgents on Indian soil. Your company wants 100% foreign ownership, and India's space regulator has already sent back one constellation application. A country of 1.4 billion is entitled to check who controls the signals over its territory.
Your own country does exactly this, and more: 1. Denied China Mobile a licence and revoked China Telecom's after nearly two decades. National security. 2. Shut out BYD with 100% tariffs and a rule barring Chinese connected-car technology. Not because of Tesla. Because Washington decided so. 3. Blocked every new foreign-made drone model, DJI included. 4. Forced TikTok into American hands. 5. Allowed Nippon Steel to buy US Steel only with a government "golden share." 6. Took a stake in Intel and a 15% cut of Nvidia's and AMD's China sales. 7. Charged $100,000 per new H-1B worker, and taxed Indian goods at up to 50% last year.
I'm not complaining. 
Sovereign states protect what they consider strategic. That isn't crony capitalism when America does it, and it isn't when India does.

But spare us the free-market sermon. According to State Department cables reported by the Washington Post, US embassies nudged tariff-hit countries to approve Starlink. America's rural broadband programme was rewritten in a way that, by the Wall Street Journal's estimate, could multiply Starlink's share several times over. When your government bends rules toward your company, it's called "tech-neutral." When ours takes its time, it's "monopolistic exploitation."

You also mocked our Prime Minister's office as a businessman's property and took sides in our domestic politics. Indians argue loudly about corporate power, political funding and cronyism. 

That's our democracy working, and it's ours to settle at our ballot box. It is not a prop for your licence negotiation.
Our villages do need connectivity. Help get it there. Finish the security compliance, accept Indian conditions on data and control, and compete on price. Indians are excellent customers of anyone who treats them as customers rather than subjects.
Thank you 🙏 for your attention on this subject matter. Now drop your weed and get back to work. 

@PMOIndia @JM_Scindia @DrSJaishankar

Your bank account got frozen overnight. No notice, no call, no FIR against you. The bank just says “cyber cell instructions.”

This is happening to ordinary people across India every day. Here is what the law actually says, and what you should do. 🧵

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). 10 अक्टूबर को दिल्ली में हुए प्रदर्शन को कवर करने के लिए इंडियन एक्सप्रेस हिंदी की टीम ग्राउंड पर मौजूद थी. शाम को लगभग 6 बजे, कवरेज के दौरान विजय और स्वाति की टीम की बातचीत एक पुलिस अधिकारी से हुई. उनके कंधे पर तीन स्टार थे और उन्होंने क्रिकेट के खेल में इस्तेमाल होने वाला हेल्मेट पहना हुआ था. 

विजय से बातचीत के दौरान उन्होंने ऐसा दर्शाया कि वो विजय को पहले से जानते थे. विजय ने मना कर दिया. पुलिस अधिकारी ने बातचीत जारी रखी. 

इतने में हमारा ध्यान उनके चश्मे पर गया. मालूम पड़ा कि उन्होंने रेबैन के मेटा ग्लासेज़ पहने हुए थे. वो शायद रिकॉर्डिंग भी कर रहे थे. सवाल पूछने पर अधिकारी ने कहा कि वो रिकॉर्डिंग नहीं कर रहे थे.

हमने अपनी फ़ुटेज चेक की तो पाया कि उसी पुलिस अधिकारी की तस्वीरें हमारे कैमरे में कैद हुई थीं. हम वो तस्वीर यहां दिखा रहे हैं.

सवाल ये हैं: 
क्या पुलिसकर्मियों को निगरानी रखने या किसी भी और इरादे से, ये स्मार्ट चश्मे दिए गए हैं? 
यदि हां, तो क्यों? 
यदि नहीं, तो क्या कोई पुलिसकर्मी, ड्यूटी के दौरान, ऐसे स्मार्ट चश्मे पहन सकता है? और लोगों की अनधिकृत रिकॉर्डिंग कर सकता है?

text:
The Supreme Court has directed that the internet “should function unhindered” in Delhi. The government and the police must obey.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) notes the order passed today by the Supreme Court of India (Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) in Shailendra Mani Tripathi v. Govind Mohan, Contempt Petition (Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026, heard with a connected habeas corpus petition. Assembling for an urgent hearing on a Sunday, the Court recorded that the petitioners had made out “a prima facie case”, issued notice to the alleged contemnors, and called for a counter affidavit and compliance report by 13 October 2026. 

At paragraph 16(c), it directed: “Internet facilities should function unhindered.” Unlike the directions on transport and movement, this one carries no qualification. The Court also directed that there shall be no illegal detention, and that lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in their work. While this direction is welcome, it should never have been necessary and does not extend to the reported and continuing instances of police violence. 

Mobile internet was reportedly suspended for twenty-four hours across a four-kilometre radius in central Delhi from 10 pm on 9 October, and counsel told the Court that about 7,000 people had been illegally detained in the city. The Union’s submission in Court was an oral assurance that internet facilities “have since been restored”. However such restoration after the fact is not accountability as under Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, a suspension order has to be published, must record its reasons, and must be proportionate and limited in duration. This was not done for the internet suspension in Delhi this week. 

IFF condemns a state of affairs in which it takes an urgent sitting of the Supreme Court and a contempt petition for the executive to be told that the internet in the national capital must stay on. We also note that  this order is only as good as its observance. Even after it was passed, we continue to notice instances in which the safety of protesters has been breached which throws into doubt whether the Union Government and the Delhi Police are observing the Court’s directions. Under Article 144 of the Constitution, all authorities, civil and judicial, are bound to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

We call upon the Union Government and the Delhi Police to:

1. Obey the Court’s directions in letter and spirit, and keep internet services in Delhi running without suspension, throttling or jamming.

2. Publish every order by which internet services were suspended in Delhi on 9 and 10 October 2026, with the reasons recorded and the findings of the Review Committee.

3. Ensure the safety of protesters, end illegal detentions, and let journalists and lawyers do their work.

4. Most importantly, respect the Constitution. The freedoms of speech and peaceful assembly under Article 19 and the guarantee of personal liberty under Article 21 are owed to every person in Delhi, including those who protest.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

On October 2nd, the government blocked BitChat in India without making the order public. We only found out through a notice on the iOS App Store.

BitChat uses Bluetooth mesh technology to pass messages from phone to phone. During Jantar Mantar 1.0, when the internet was shut and blocking vans jammed even SMS, protesters used it to find each other and share water and medicines.

Calling it a national security threat makes little sense. It only works over short distances, and the block only stops new downloads. Anyone can install it across the border and come back. The only people affected are citizens exercising their right to peaceful assembly.

What’s next, walkie-talkies and carrier pigeons? We’re filing RTIs and will keep pushing for transparency.

Statement: MeitY’s “enhanced diligence” advisory pressures platforms to police protest speech. It must be withdrawn.

October 9, 2026

On October 8, MeitY’s Cyber Laws Division sent an advisory to all social media intermediaries. It asks them to exercise “enhanced diligence” over false, misleading, manipulated or out-of-context content linked to “ongoing public events and developments”, to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information, to label or “contextualise” misleading content, and to prioritise complaints from “authorised Government agencies” on public-order content. It takes effect immediately. MeitY has not published it and its text became public through MediaNama. It was issued as citizens protest in Delhi and Mumbai over the revision of electoral rolls, with a protest called at Jantar Mantar for October 10. We call on MEITY to withdraw it.

First, the advisory names no provision that empowers MeitY to issue it and such advisories are not issued under any law. Section 79(2)(c) of the IT Act conditions safe harbour on “due diligence” and on guidelines the Central Government may “prescribe”, that is, by rules notified and laid before Parliament under Section 87. The IT Rules recognise only “due diligence” under Rule 3 and “additional due diligence” for significant social media intermediaries under Rule 4. The phrase, “Enhanced diligence” used in this Advisory appears in neither. Further, MeitY’s proposed Rule 3(4) in the last round of Amendments mooted to the IT Rules, 2021, which has not been notified further confirms this does not have any legal character. Second, an advisory cannot alter the application of existing law. Rule 3(1)(b)(v) covers only misinformation communicated “knowingly and intentionally” that is “patently false and untrue or misleading in nature”. The advisory drops both qualifiers and adds “social tranquility”, neither that nor “misleading” is a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).

Third, facing an undefined standard platforms will censor more than the law requires. The advisory asks them to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information and to “strengthen their existing monitoring”. This is proactive monitoring by another name, which the Rules contemplate only for narrow categories such as child sexual abuse material. Further, it is vague and does does not define “authorised Government agencies” or “priority”, and does not require platforms to tell users that a government complaint lay behind an action. Users will see only a platform decision. The State’s role disappears, and with it any route to challenge that role in court. The advisory governs public speech but is not itself public. It cites no statutory provision, is approved by an unnamed “competent authority”, and does not identify the events or content that prompted it.

We anticipate a huge spike in censorship over the next few days.

We call on MeitY to:
1. Publish the advisory in full, including any clause (v), and state the provision under which it was issued.
2. Withdraw it, or clarify that it creates no obligations beyond the IT Act and Rules and that “enhanced diligence” is not a condition of safe harbour.
3. Disclose which agencies are sending complaints under it, and how many.
4. Abandon the proposed Rule 3(4).

We also call on platforms to:
1. Disclose all government complaints and requests received under this advisory.
2. Act only on requests that meet the Shreya Singhal standard and Rule 3(1)(d).
3. Refrain from proactively filtering or downranking protest content on the basis of this advisory.
4. Notify affected users, including when an action follows a government complaint.

PS: We got the text of the advisory from @medianama' s website.
